source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false items when the format is right. Calibration improves with model size and with few-shot prompts.
numbers: 52B-scale Anthropic models. Fig 1 pools 5 sampling tasks (TriviaQA, Lambada, arithmetic, GSM8k, Codex) with equal weight.
limits: Replacing an option with 'none of the above' cuts accuracy and calibration a lot. RLHF policies look miscalibrated until a temperature adjustment is applied.
agent_relevance: Calibration depends on answer format, so a confidence guardrail should fix the format and not rely on free text.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know (P(True))
finding: A model can judge whether its own sampled answer is right (P(True)). It works better when several of its own samples are shown (k-shot), mostly by improving calibration rather than discrimination.
numbers: Fig 1 right: accuracy on each task rises when only questions with P(True)>0.5 are kept. 20-shot self-evaluation used.
limits: Self-evaluation is harder than judging others, because models find their own samples more plausible. Zero-shot it is poorly calibrated.
agent_relevance: Own-answer self-check gives a usable but biased signal. Use it only after a code-checked step.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know (P(IK))
finding: A head trained to predict 'I know the answer' (P(IK)) works in distribution and partly transfers to new tasks. P(IK) rises when relevant source text or hints are in the context.
numbers: Trained on TriviaQA, arithmetic, Python synthesis and Lambada; OOD histograms in Fig 2; also tested with GSM8k hints.
limits: The authors say the model 'struggles with calibration of P(IK) on new tasks'. Needs training, so it is not prompt-only.
agent_relevance: A cheap 'do I know this' gate is possible if we ever fine-tune. For a scaffold-only agent it is a design target.

source: Lin, Hilton, Evans (2022) Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words
finding: GPT-3 fine-tuned on 100 labelled questions per sub-task can say a confidence in words ('verbalized probability') that stays calibrated across arithmetic task families. Reported as the first calibrated words about own answers.
numbers: CalibratedMath: 21 arithmetic tasks. Table 1 (MSE, lower better), trained on Add-subtract: Multi-answer verbalized about 22.0 vs constant baseline 37.4; Multiply-divide verbalized about 10.4 vs constant 11.7.
limits: Gain under shift on Multiply-divide is small (about 1 point of MSE over a constant). Needs fine-tuning. Arithmetic only. The table text is garbled in the PDF extraction, so row labels were matched with care.
agent_relevance: Words can carry real confidence, but only after training. A prompt-only agent should not assume this.

source: Lin, Hilton, Evans (2022) Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words (latent evidence)
finding: The calibration seems to come from pre-trained latent features that track uncertainty over the answer, not from imitating human hedging. Verbalized and logit-based confidence both generalize under shift.
numbers: Compared answer logit (zero-shot), indirect logit (fine-tuned) and verbalized numbers in Fig 4 and Table 1.
limits: One model family (GPT-3), one domain.
agent_relevance: Supports reading confidence from model state, not from the tone of text.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation
finding: Verbalized confidence from GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Vicuna is overconfident and weak at telling right from wrong answers.
numbers: Average ECE above 0.377 for GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and Vicuna. GPT-4 has lower ECE but average AUROC only 62.7% (chance 50%). About 22.2% AUROC gain from GPT-3 to GPT-4. 5 models, 8 tasks.
limits: Prompt-based. Tasks needing professional knowledge are the worst.
agent_relevance: Never read a stated '90% sure' as a probability. Use it as a weak rank signal at most.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation (human-inspired prompts)
finding: Prompts borrowed from human metacognition (self-probing, step-by-step confidence, Top-K guesses) cut overconfidence partly. Sampling several answers and aggregating agreement helps more for failure prediction.
numbers: Five prompt strategies on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. White-box vs black-box AUROC gap is narrow, 0.522 to 0.605 in the abstract.
limits: Gains shrink on GPT-4. No method wins everywhere.
agent_relevance: Agreement between several independent attempts is the best black-box signal. Our schema already counts votes in code.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: For RLHF chat models, confidence they write out is better calibrated than their token probabilities. Relative ECE drops by over 50% in many cases.
numbers: ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude 1 and 2 on TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA. In the table read: TriviaQA label-prob ECE 0.140 vs verbalized top-1 0.068 and top-2 0.050; AUC 0.869 vs 0.879 and 0.894. TruthfulQA ECE 0.451 vs 0.361 (top-2), AUC 0.418 vs 0.485.
limits: Conflicts in tone with Xiong 2024 and Kapoor 2024, who find verbalized confidence overconfident or weak. Raw ECE can hide poor discrimination (TruthfulQA AUC near 0.5). The table read here is the first one; the model for it was not confirmed.
agent_relevance: Asking for the top 2 guesses with probabilities is a cheap prompt change that improved ECE. Recheck on our own model.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know
finding: Prompting alone is not enough for good uncertainty. Fine-tuning on about 1,000 graded right or wrong answers (LoRA) beats prompting, sampling and probes in ECE and AUROC.
numbers: LLaMA-2 7B/13B, Mistral 7B, open-ended MMLU. Prompt methods do not improve calibration as base models get better. AUROC improves a little with scale. Sampling gives good ECE but weak AUROC. Verbal elicitation has decent AUROC but poor ECE even after temperature scaling.
limits: Open-weights models only. Needs 1k graded labels and training.
agent_relevance: If we ever train, 1k graded examples is the budget. Without training, treat verbal confidence on open-ended tasks as unreliable.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) user study
finding: People use calibrated confidence scores when deciding whether to accept a model answer, and ignore random ones.
numbers: N = 181 participants (about 20 per variant), multiple-choice exam with Mistral 7B Instruct. Largest reliance difference with LoRA+Probe scores; the random-score baseline did not change reliance.
limits: Preliminary study, one small model, crowdsourced.
agent_relevance: A shown confidence only helps users if it is reliable.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What Large Language Models Know and What People Think They Know
finding: Users overestimate how often LLM answers are right when they read default explanations. Model confidence is much better calibrated than human confidence in the model.
numbers: 301 participants over Experiments 1 and 2. Model AUC: GPT-3.5 0.751, PaLM2 0.746 (multiple choice), GPT-4o 0.781 (short answer). Human AUC on default explanations only 0.589, 0.602 and 0.592.
limits: Trivia and MMLU-style questions only.
agent_relevance: The text around an answer leaks confidence to the reader. The final prose should not sound more sure than the checked state.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What Large Language Models Know and What People Think They Know (explanation length and fix)
finding: Longer explanations raise user confidence even when accuracy does not improve. Matching explanation wording to the model's internal confidence narrows both the calibration gap and the discrimination gap.
numbers: Discrimination gap narrowed, Bayes factors above 100 (Exp 2a and 2c) and 6.48 (2b).
limits: The fix needs a good internal confidence signal.
agent_relevance: Tie the wording and length of the final answer to a measured score.

source: Steyvers and Peters (2025) Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Humans and Large Language Models
finding: Review mapping human metacognition (sensitivity, calibration, meta-d') onto LLMs. Token-likelihood confidence tracks accuracy trial by trial better than verbalized confidence.
numbers: Example figure: GPT-3.5 token-likelihood confidence on MMLU is overconfident (AUC 0.778). A GPT-4.1-mini fine-tuned to give verbal confidence on TriviaQA reached AUC 0.83 and better calibration.
limits: Review plus illustrative examples, not a new full experiment. Notes that metrics other than meta-d' are contaminated by Type-1 accuracy.
agent_relevance: Supplies the vocabulary (sensitivity vs calibration) and tells us what to measure.

source: Cacioli (2026) Do LLMs Know What They Know? Measuring Metacognitive Efficiency with Signal Detection Theory
finding: Calibration scores mix 'how much it knows' with 'how well confidence tracks it'. A signal-detection split finds metacognitive information varies about 2-fold across four 7B-9B models, and temperature changes accuracy but leaves metacognitive information near flat for three of four models.
numbers: 224,000 factual QA trials, 4 models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Llama-3-8B-Base, Gemma-2-9B-Instruct). Range 1.98 fold. Rank correlation with accuracy -0.80 (TriviaQA) and +0.00 (Natural Questions). z-ROC slopes 0.78 to 1.18. Abstention gain tracks meta-information (rho=+1.00).
limits: Independent single-author, pre-registered. v3 corrects a scorer bias (it missed 53% and 26% of two models' correct answers), and the earlier inverse accuracy-efficiency claim did not survive. Small models, token log-prob confidence.
agent_relevance: A live example of a correction in this field. Also: a confidence gate pays off exactly as far as the confidence signal is informative.

source: Dai and Wang (2026) Beyond 0-100: How Confidence Scale Design Shapes Verbalized Confidence and LLM Metacognition
finding: Verbalized 0-100 confidence clusters on round numbers. A 0-20 scale gave better metacognitive efficiency (meta-d' based) than 0-100 in the tested models.
numbers: 6 primary LLMs, 3 datasets, plus 1 extra model. The three most frequent values hold 78.2% to 92.1% of answers on the 0-100 scale. Baseline M-ratio runs from 0.62 (Qwen3-30B) to 0.92 (GPT-5.2). Confidence entropy 0.95 to 1.88 bits. Temperature 0.
limits: Holds only within the evaluated models, datasets and prompts. Harsh boundary compression hurts. Round-number bias persists on irregular ranges.
agent_relevance: Cheap change: ask for confidence on a short scale. Test it on our model.

source: Kumaran et al. (2025) How Overconfidence in Initial Choices and Underconfidence Under Criticism Modulate Change of Mind in LLMs
finding: Models cling to their first answer when it is visible, and overreact to opposing advice. Gemma 3, GPT-4o and o1-preview show a choice-supportive bias.
numbers: Mean change-of-mind rate 32.5% with the answer hidden vs 13.1% shown. With opposing advice: 85.0% hidden vs 39.2% shown. Confidence at which change-of-mind fell under 50% was 0.77, 0.92, 0.96 for advice accuracy 50, 60, 70%. Inconsistent advice is overweighted relative to a Bayesian update.
limits: Mostly binary city-latitude tasks, plus SimpleQA and GSM-MC subsets. Three model families.
agent_relevance: Strong reason to hide earlier answers when re-judging (blind verify). Order of critique matters.

source: Prasad and Nguyen (2025) When Two LLMs Debate, Both Think They'll Win
finding: In debates against each other, models start overconfident and raise confidence as rounds go on instead of lowering it.
numbers: 60 three-round debates, 10 models. Initial confidence 72.9% vs rational 50%. Final round about 83%. Both sides claimed at least 75% in 61.7% of debates. Identical copies rose from 64.1% to 75.2%. Told the chance was exactly 50%, confidence still rose from 50.0% to 57.1%.
limits: Zero-sum debate, not factual QA. Private scratchpad confidence sometimes differed from the public number.
agent_relevance: Confidence climbs just from continuing to argue. Never keep a running self-reported confidence across turns.

source: Ou et al. (2025) BrowseConf: Confidence-Guided Test-Time Scaling for Web Agents
finding: Search agents' verbalized confidence after a long run is overconfident but ranks answers well. Accuracy is near zero below 70% confidence and more than double the average above 95%.
numbers: BrowseComp with DeepSeek-V3.1 and gpt-oss-120b. Best bin 90-94%: only 53.33% accuracy for DeepSeek-V3.1. Reported 30.0% vs 30.49% here, so asking for confidence did not cost accuracy.
limits: Open agentic models, one benchmark family. Overconfident in absolute terms.
agent_relevance: Use confidence as a stop-or-retry gate, not as a probability.

source: Ou et al. (2025) BrowseConf (confidence-gated retries)
finding: Retrying until confidence passes a threshold gives similar or better accuracy at lower cost than fixed-budget voting. Carrying a summary of failed attempts cuts later work.
numbers: Table 1 BrowseComp / BrowseComp-zh, accuracy / attempts: Self-Consistency (10) 36.7 / 10 and 59.9 / 10; BrowseConf-Zero 41.3 / 5.67 and 59.2 / 3.43; BrowseConf-Neg 41.8 / 5.72 and 54.3 / 3.68.
limits: Threshold choice matters: too strict adds cost without gain. On BC-ZH none beat self-consistency (59.2 and 54.3 vs 59.9).
agent_relevance: Direct precedent for a confidence-gated loop in an LLM agent. The gain is mostly saved compute.

source: Xuan et al. (2026) The Confidence Dichotomy: Miscalibration in Tool-Use Agents
finding: Evidence tools (web search) cause severe overconfidence. Verification tools (code interpreter) ground reasoning and reduce miscalibration. A calibration-aware RL method (CAR) cut ECE.
numbers: ECE relative reductions up to 68% with CAR, using a Brier-weighted reward (weight 1/3). Full Brier weight (plain RLCR) gave lowest ECE but lost accuracy. Also tested with the Serper API on SimpleQA-verified.
limits: Needs RL training. Per-model numbers not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Prefer code-checked verification as the confidence source. Treat a raw web hit as weak evidence that inflates confidence.

source: Damani et al. (2026) Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty (RLCR)
finding: Adding a Brier term to the correctness reward trains reasoning models that stay accurate and become calibrated. Correctness-only RL worsens calibration.
numbers: The paper's own summary: ECE of 0.37 on HotpotQA and 0.26 on a math collection (RLVR) drops sharply with RLCR in domain. Out of domain RLVR hurts calibration while RLCR improves it. Confidence-weighted voting at test time raises accuracy.
limits: Training method. The proof holds for bounded proper scoring rules only (log loss fails). Exact RLCR ECE per set was not read from the table.
agent_relevance: If we ever train, use a Brier reward. At test time, weight votes by stated confidence.

source: Mei et al. (2025) Reasoning about Uncertainty: Do Reasoning Models Know When They Don't Know?
finding: Reasoning models are overconfident, and more so with deeper reasoning. Re-checking their own chain of thought (introspective UQ) helps some models and hurts others.
numbers: Verbalized confidence often above 85% even for wrong answers. Introspection improves o3-Mini and DeepSeek R1 but leaves Claude 3.7 Sonnet worse calibrated.
limits: Effect is model specific. Numbers taken from the abstract and intro.
agent_relevance: Do not assume more thinking improves confidence. Measure on the model used.

source: Barkan et al. (2025) Do Large Language Models Know What They Are Capable Of?
finding: All tested LLMs are overconfident about their own task success, though most beat chance at predicting it. In multi-step agent tasks overconfidence gets worse as the task goes on.
numbers: BigCodeBench: newer or larger models usually do not discriminate better, though Claude models trend upward. Over 9 contracts, GPT-4.1's predicted success hardly changed and Sonnet 3.5 became somewhat less overconfident.
limits: Specific task suites. Effects of failure experience vary by model.
agent_relevance: Success forecasts from the model itself are optimistic. Replace with measured pass rates.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Agentic Confidence Calibration (Holistic Trajectory Calibration)
finding: Confidence read from the whole agent trajectory beats last-step confidence. A small interpretable model on trajectory features improves calibration and discrimination.
numbers: Eight benchmarks. On GPQA the baselines had ECE about 0.41 to 0.45 and HTC-Reduced with temperature 0.136; on SimpleQA HTC reached ECE 0.077 with AUROC 0.69. GPQA AUROC about 0.64.
limits: Needs a labelled calibration set per agent. On HLE ECE stays high, about 0.43.
agent_relevance: Log trajectory features (steps, retries, disagreement) and fit a tiny calibrator in code, outside the model.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without outside feedback, asking a model to re-check its own answer does not help and often hurts.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after round 1 of self-correction; GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 then 89.0 after more rounds. With oracle labels GPT-4 GSM8K reaches 97.5.
limits: Prompted self-correction on reasoning tasks. Oracle gain is not realistic.
agent_relevance: Self-monitoring without a ground-truth check is not reliable. Matches the rule that the model never grades itself without a check.

source: Yin et al. (2023) Do Large Language Models Know What They Don't Know? (SelfAware)
finding: Models have some self-knowledge of unanswerable questions but fall short of humans. Instructions and examples raise it.
numbers: F1 on detecting unanswerable questions: GPT-4 75.47% vs human 84.93%. In-context examples lifted GPT-4 to 42.64% in one measure and text-ada-001 from 2.48% to 10.61%.
limits: Built dataset (SelfAware); detection by uncertainty cues in responses. Which measure gave 42.64% was not pinned down.
agent_relevance: Abstaining on unanswerable questions is possible but below human level, so keep a code-side abstention rule.

source: Manakul, Liusie, Gales (2023) SelfCheckGPT
finding: Sampling several answers and checking that each sentence is backed by the others finds hallucinations with no outside database.
numbers: Sentence-level AUC-PR: non-factual detection 72.96 (random) to 83.21 with GPT-3 token probabilities; factual sentences 27.04 to 53.97. Passage-level correlation also reported.
limits: Table rows were hard to align in the PDF extraction; the numbers used are the ones quoted in the text. Black-box proxy-model scores were lower.
agent_relevance: Agreement among samples is a working monitor for an LLM agent loop.

source: Fleming and Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition (meta-d' framework, as cited by Cacioli 2026 and Dai 2026)
finding: Source of meta-d' and M-ratio = meta-d'/d', which separate metacognitive efficiency from task accuracy. Both 2026 LLM papers apply it.
numbers: Not opened this session; see the Dai and Cacioli lines for LLM uses (M-ratio 0.62 to 0.92).
limits: Defined for two-alternative tasks, so not well defined for open-ended QA (Cacioli).
agent_relevance: Use meta-d' for binary checks only. For open QA use AUROC.
